title: In what sense efficacy depends on free choice
source_text: CXXXIV. Caeterum quanquam authores illius sententiae efficaciam gratiae velint esse aliquid in auxilio divino, quod voluntatis operationem antecedit; ac proinde quod ab ejus consensu & cooperatione ea ratione non pendet, ut in hominis potestate situm sit gratiam vel efficacem, vel inefficacem reddere, ut volunt Molina, & qui eum sequuntur: nihilominus non negant gratiae efficaciam a libero arbitrio aliquo modo pendere. Etenim, juxta ipsos, efficacia gratiae duobus modis considerari potest, vel in actu primo, vel in actu secundo. Priori modo spectata ea nihil aliud est, quam vis efficiendi, quae non distinguitur ab ipso auxilio: & hac ratione efficacia gratiae non pendet a libero arbitrio, sed a Deo. Posteriori modo efficacia gratiae sumitur pro ipsa efficientia, seu influxu actuali gratiae in opus supernaturale. Et sub hac etiam consideratione efficacia gratiae pendet a Deo. Sicut enim influxus instrumenti in opus pendet ab agente principali, quod tali instrumento utitur: ita influxus gratiae in opus supernaturale pendet a Deo, ut ab agente primario, quod per gratiam, ut per instrumentum quoddam suum, operatur. Verum quia haec actualis efficientia gratiae, non tantum pendet a Deo, sed etiam ab ipso libero arbitrio, ut a causa partiali, sine cujus operatione gratia non ageret, ideo dicunt hoc respectu, id est, in actu secundo, gratiae efficaciam etiam a libero arbitrio pendere. Quemadmodum ea de re mentem suam explicat Petrus a Sancto Joseph in tractatu de gratia divina disput. 7. num. 62.
pass_a_gloss: CXXXIV. But although the authors of that opinion will have the efficacy of grace be something in the divine aid, which precedes the operation of the will; and therefore which does not depend on its consent & cooperation in such a way, that it is placed in man's power to render grace either efficacious, or inefficacious, as Molina will have it, & those who follow him: nevertheless they do not deny that the efficacy of grace depends in some way on free choice. For, according to them, the efficacy of grace can be considered in two ways, either in first act, or in second act. Regarded in the former way it is nothing else, than the power of effecting, which is not distinguished from the aid itself: & in this respect the efficacy of grace does not depend on free choice, but on God. In the latter way the efficacy of grace is taken for the very efficiency, or actual influence of grace on the supernatural work. And under this consideration also the efficacy of grace depends on God. For as the influence of an instrument on the work depends on the principal agent, which uses such an instrument: so the influence of grace on the supernatural work depends on God, as on the primary agent, who works through grace, as through a certain instrument of his own. But because this actual efficiency of grace, depends not only on God, but also on free choice itself, as on a partial cause, without whose operation grace would not act, therefore they say that in this respect, that is, in second act, the efficacy of grace depends also on free choice. As Peter of Saint Joseph explains his mind on this matter in the treatise on divine grace disput. 7. num. 62.
pass_b_english: Thesis CXXXIV. The authors of this view hold that the efficacy of grace is something in the divine aid that comes before the will's working, and so does not hang on the will's consent and cooperation in the way Molina and his followers claim, as though it lay in a person's power to make grace efficacious or inefficacious. Even so, they do not deny that the efficacy of grace depends on free choice in some way. On their account it can be considered in two ways, in first act or in second act. Taken the first way, it is simply the power to bring about the effect, which is not distinct from the aid itself; in this respect it depends not on free choice but on God.

Taken the second way, efficacy means the actual working itself, the actual influence of grace on the supernatural work; and in this respect too it depends on God. Just as an instrument's influence on a work depends on the principal agent using it, so the influence of grace on a supernatural work depends on God as primary agent, who works through grace as through an instrument of his own. Yet this actual working of grace depends not only on God but also on free choice itself, as a partial cause without whose operation grace would not act. In this respect, then, that is, in second act, they say the efficacy of grace also depends on free choice. So Peter of Saint Joseph explains his mind on the matter in the treatise on divine grace, disputation 7, number 62.

choices.why: Scholastic pair: first act is the power to act (here the aid's force to effect); second act is the actual exercise (the aid's actual influence on the work).
